primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- CJP's Philconsa Constitution Day address explaining the Chief Justice's two roles, as primus inter pares in the Supreme Court and as leader and chief executive officer of the entire judiciary, and how both serve the Philconsa creed to preserve and defend the Constitution
His one-sentence judicial philosophy: to safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of the people while upholding the rule of law and the independence of the judiciary

The asymmetry at the heart of that philosophy -- strict scrutiny and a heavy presumption of invalidity for laws restricting civil liberties, especially of the poor, but judicial deference and a laissez-faire stance toward the political branches on economic policy

His leadership program: a judiciary characterized by four Ins -- integrity, independence, intelligence and industry -- and judicial reform aimed at the four items code-named ACID: limited access to justice, corruption, incompetence and delay
sub_topics: He thanks the Philconsa officers, congratulates the governors he has just inducted, and recalls its distinguished past presidents from Sergio Osmeña Sr. to Justices Bautista, Paredes and Regala
'Triple Twenty-One': on the 21st of December 2005 at 2:56 p.m. he took his oath as the 21st Chief Justice, the first sworn in during the 21st century, in a ceremony lasting less than three minutes

As primus inter pares he presides over en banc sessions, controls the flow of proceedings, shapes the agenda, opens discussion and summarizes arguments -- yet, like his fourteen colleagues, holds only one vote
Even Chief Justices from Arellano to Davide have found themselves in the minority, thanks to the absolute freedom of discussion and choice that justices enjoy

His record is open to scrutiny: decisions published in the Philippine Reports and SCRA, the fully searchable e-library launched on November 19, 2004, and ten books, one for each year of his incumbency

Safeguarding liberty: the 1987 Constitution is promotive of social justice, responsive to women, protective of labor, cognizant of indigenous cultural communities and respectful of human rights, and even grants the Court quasi-legislative power to promulgate rules protecting constitutional rights
Ang Bagong Bayani-OFW Labor Party v. Comelec, which he wrote, resting the party-list system on the principle that those who have less in life should have more in law
Laws impinging on fundamental rights come with a heavy presumption against constitutional validity, and restrictions on freedom of expression are particularly suspect and subject to strict scrutiny

Public opinion polling as protected expression: ABS-CBN v. Comelec, where the Court declared it would lean in favor of freedom in borderline situations, reiterated in Social Weather Stations v. Comelec, and traced back to United States v. Bustos in 1918

The counterpart rule for prosperity: deference to the political branches on economic policy, as in Tañada v. Angara on trade liberalization and globalization and La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, which Raul C. Pangalangan, citing Larry Kramer, called 'popular constitutionalism'

The limit of that deference: the Court will still strike down any policy or act that clearly violates the Constitution, the laws or settled jurisprudence, or that is issued with arbitrariness, whim, caprice, bias or personal hostility

The second role: although the Constitution lodges management in the Court en banc, resolutions, laws, traditions and practice make the Chief Justice the judiciary's chief executive officer, looked to by 2,000 judges and 26,000 personnel
The tension he names between jurist and leader -- detached, unreachable and bound by precedent on one side; transparent, accountable and obliged to re-engineer and innovate on the other
Integrity as more than honesty: moral courage to denounce wrong, intellectual decency, indifference to acclaim, and impartiality that avoids undue social contact with litigants and lawyers

Independence as freedom from the 'ships' -- kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship -- and from misplaced gratitude to the appointing authority, President, Congress, media, critics and litigants
His formulation that the strength of the judiciary lies not in brute power or money but in moral courage: 'Its might is in its being right'

Industry measured against a backbreaking docket -- about 6,000 pending cases, roughly 400 per justice, 25 to 30 new cases monthly, at least 30 dispositions a month -- and the constitutional deadlines of 3, 12 and 24 months
Intelligence as both knowledge and wisdom: mastery of law joined to familiarity with all branches of knowledge

Judicial reform: the Action Program for Judicial Reform begun by Davide and hailed as a model at the November 28-30, 2005 International Conference and Showcase on Judicial Reforms, which made the Philippine Supreme Court the world secretariat and repository of reform initiatives and gave it the JRN21 website

The conclusion answering doubters of a short term: Christmas comes one day a year yet reverberates for all time, and the two bronze statues at Padre Faura honor both Cayetano Arellano, who served nearly twenty years, and the martyred Jose Abad Santos, who served barely six months

stances.claim: In cases involving civil liberties the scales should weigh heavily in favor of the people, especially the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak, so that laws impinging on fundamental rights carry a heavy presumption against constitutional validity and restrictions on expression face strict scrutiny.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-text inventory followed by his own decisions as illustrations, culminating in an explicit statement of belief

stances.claim: In conflicts over prosperity and development, deference must be accorded the political branches: courts should not pass upon the merits or wisdom of trade liberalization and economic globalization, which the people have left to the President and Congress to evaluate and decide.
stances.rhetorical_move: symmetrical counterpart to the liberty rule, grounded in Tañada v. Angara and relabelled by a commentator as popular constitutionalism

stances.claim: Judicial independence requires magistrates to be free of the 'ships' that plague public service -- kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship -- and of any misplaced gratitude to the appointing or recommending authority, and the judiciary's real strength lies not in brute power or money but in moral courage: its might is in its being right.
stances.rhetorical_move: aphoristic definition, contrasting the judiciary's lack of army and purse with the authority of being right

stances.claim: A short term need not make a Chief Justice a mere footnote, since greatness is measured not by length of service but by one's real contribution to instilling lasting values and nurturing a reformed and transformed judiciary.
stances.rhetorical_move: answering the skeptics' question directly, then arguing by analogy from Christmas and from the two bronze statues at Padre Faura

notable_anecdotes: The 'Triple Twenty-One' moment: on December 21, 2005, as the clock struck 2:56 p.m., he took his oath as the 21st Chief Justice, the first sworn in during the 21st century, in a Malacañang ceremony that lasted less than three minutes.
He notes that he has written ten books, one for every year of his decade on the Supreme Court, covering subjects from mathematics to the biosciences to new economic paradigms.
He cites the Court's fully searchable e-library, launched on November 19, 2004 and the first of its kind in the region, holding every decision since the Court's founding in 1901.
He describes the backbreaking docket -- about 6,000 pending cases, some 400 per justice, 25 to 30 new cases raffled monthly, requiring each justice to dispose of at least 30 cases a month.

He reports that the November 2005 International Conference and Showcase voted the Philippine Supreme Court the world's secretariat and repository of judicial reform initiatives, and that APJR administrator Evelyn Toledo Dumdum had been asked by the Russian and Armenian Supreme Courts to help set up their own reform offices.
He pauses mid-speech to note that he has already used up 30 minutes and cannot discuss the ACID program in the further 30 minutes it would need -- 'a luxury I do not have tonight.'

He closes by pointing to the two giant bronze statues at the entrance of the Supreme Court on Padre Faura: Cayetano Arellano, who served nearly twenty years, and Jose Abad Santos, who served barely six months.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' is CJP's Philconsa Constitution Day address, delivered soon after he took his oath on December 21, 2005 at 2:56 p.m. as the 21st Chief Justice, the first sworn in during the 21st century. He organized the speech around the Chief Justice's two roles. As primus inter pares he presides over en banc sessions, shapes the agenda, opens discussion and summarizes arguments, yet holds only one vote, and even Chief Justices from Arellano to Davide have found themselves in the minority. Pointing to published reports, the Court's e-library and the ten books he wrote over ten years, he summarized his judicial philosophy in a sentence: to safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of the people while upholding the rule of law and the independence of the judiciary. On liberty he stressed that the 1987 Constitution protects social justice, labor, women, indigenous communities and human rights, invoked his own ruling in Ang Bagong Bayani that those who have less in life should have more in law, and traced a line of free-expression cases -- ABS-CBN, Social Weather Stations, and United States v. Bustos -- in which the Court leans in favor of freedom. On prosperity he urged deference to the political branches, citing Tañada v. Angara and La Bugal-B'laan, while reserving the power to strike down acts that clearly violate the Constitution or are arbitrary. Turning to his second role as leader of some 2,000 judges and 26,000 personnel, he set out the four Ins -- integrity, independence, intelligence and industry -- describing independence as freedom from kinship, relationship, friendship and fellowship, and declaring that the judiciary's might is in its being right. He named ACID as his reform agenda, reported the international standing won by the Action Program for Judicial Reform, and closed by answering doubts about his short term with the statues of Arellano and Abad Santos.
